The death certificate's informant (son-in-law James Brown) had no firsthand knowledge of a birth event roughly 63 years prior; this weakens the Pennsylvania claim, but no preferred assertion is formally recorded yet.

Until that candidate is eliminated or the correct Patrick linked to the 1908 certificate, the parentage conclusion rests on an unverified identity chain.

**Events the prior timeline held that this one drops:** none — all four events are carried forward. The gap boundary `1860-01-01` has been corrected to `1860`; the 1890 census has been removed from expected events (destroyed); standard places and distances have been added throughout.

Next steps: Use question-selection to plan the 1870, 1880, and 1900 census searches (closes the high-severity gap and may resolve c_002 by confirming only one Patrick Flynn persists in Schuylkill County). Patrick Flynn's documented life, laid out in order, runs from an estimated birth around 1845 in Ireland, through two census appearances as a child and teenager in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household in 1850 and 1860, and then goes completely silent until his death on 12 March 1908 in the same county. That middle stretch — nearly half a century, covering his adult life, probable marriage (a son-in-law signed the death certificate), and every working year — has produced no records yet. The silence is not evidence he stayed put or vanished; it is an unresearched gap that the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses could fill. Two complications hang over the whole picture: it is not yet settled whether Patrick was born in Ireland (what the censuses say) or Pennsylvania (what the death certificate says), and there is a second Patrick Flynn of nearly the same age living in the same county in 1850, which means it is not yet formally confirmed that the boy in Thomas Flynn's household is the same man who died in 1908.

The next step is to search the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County, which will both fill the long gap and provide the evidence needed to sort out the two identity questions.
